opus-5.5.text:
I think post-training matters more and more now. In the past, many people saw the base model as where most of the intelligence came from, and post-training as a kind of alignment layer: making the model follow instructions, be safer, and sound nicer. That view is outdated.

Pre-training gives you a very strong prior. It compresses a huge amount of human knowledge into the model, and that is still the foundation. But high-quality natural data is limited. You can't just keep scaling tokens forever and expect the same returns. So the question becomes: where does the next order of magnitude of capability come from? A big part of the answer is post-training, especially reinforcement learning.

With RL, the model isn't just imitating what humans wrote. It can explore, try things, get feedback, and improve on tasks where you can define a good reward, like math, coding, and increasingly agentic tasks where the model has to take many steps, use tools, and recover from its own mistakes. That gives you a way to generate new learning signal that isn't capped by existing human data. In a sense, it's a way to keep scaling when pre-training data becomes the bottleneck.

For our current base model, I see post-training doing a few things. First, unlocking capabilities that are latent in the base model but not reliably expressed, like long chains of reasoning. Second, teaching genuinely new behaviors through RL, especially long-horizon tasks. Third, shaping the model's taste and style, which people underestimate. A model's taste is a big part of what users actually feel.

There are real challenges, though. Reward design is hard. If your reward is imperfect, the model will find shortcuts, and in long-horizon tasks the feedback is sparse and noisy. Many tasks we care about, like writing or open-ended research, don't have a clean verifier, so you need better ways to evaluate them, sometimes using models to judge models, which brings its own problems.

So I don't see pre-training and post-training as two separate stages anymore. They're one system. The base model determines the ceiling of what RL can explore, and RL determines how much of that potential you actually realize. Going forward, I expect a larger and larger share of compute to go into post-training, and the teams that do RL at scale well will have a real advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training can unlock capabilities latent in the base model and that RL determines how much of its potential is realized.

fable-5.1.text:
Post-training is where a lot of the real leverage is right now, but I'd frame it a bit differently from how people usually talk about it. Pre-training gives you the ceiling. It determines what knowledge and what latent capabilities exist inside the model. Post-training is how you actually reach that ceiling, and in some cases, through reinforcement learning, how you push beyond what you'd get from imitation alone.

For our current base model, I think of post-training in three layers. The first is the basic alignment layer, making the model follow instructions, be helpful, be safe. That part is relatively mature in the industry now. The second layer is reasoning. This is where reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has changed the game. If you have a good base model and you let it explore long chains of thought, with rewards from math, code, or other domains where you can check the answer, the model genuinely gets better at thinking, not just at sounding like it thinks. We've seen that scaling the RL compute here behaves a lot like scaling pre-training compute did a few years ago. There's a clear curve, and we're still early on it.

The third layer, and the one I'm most focused on, is agentic capability. Long-horizon tasks, tool use, working inside a real environment over many steps, recovering from mistakes. This is much harder to post-train for because the reward is sparse and the environments are expensive to build. But I believe this is where the next big jump in usefulness comes from. A model that can take a vague goal and work for an hour, or a day, and come back with something finished.

One thing I'd emphasize: post-training and pre-training are not independent. The data and signals you discover in RL feed back into what you want the next base model to see. So I don't see post-training as a finishing step. It's more like one half of a loop, and the quality of the base model determines how far the loop can take you.

r001.rationale: The candidate says pre-training sets the model’s ceiling and post-training is how the model reaches that ceiling, framing it as realizing the base model’s performance potential.

astra-6.text:
I think further post-training is very important, but its role depends on what you want to improve. The base model gives you a starting point—a set of capabilities learned during pre-training. Post-training helps turn those capabilities into behavior that is useful: following instructions, reasoning through a problem, and recognizing when the model doesn’t have enough information.

And with reinforcement learning, the ambition is to go beyond adjusting how the model answers. If we can provide a reliable signal for whether it succeeds, we can train it to solve problems more effectively. The challenge is making sure that improvement generalizes, rather than just making the model better at the particular tasks we reward.

So I see pre-training and post-training as complementary. We want a strong base model, and then we want to understand how much further we can push it with the right objectives and feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says post-training helps realize the base model’s capabilities and asks how much further it can be pushed with suitable objectives and feedback, conveying its role in reaching the model’s performance potential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think post-training is very important, but its role depends on what the base model already knows. Pretraining gives you a foundation of knowledge and capabilities. Post-training helps turn those capabilities into something useful: following instructions, reasoning through problems, and interacting with users more reliably.

The interesting question is how far we can push beyond simply shaping the model’s responses. If we can give it tasks with reliable feedback, then reinforcement learning can help it discover better ways to solve problems. That makes post-training a way to develop capabilities as well as expose them.

So I see pretraining and post-training as complementary. We need to keep improving the base model, while also building better training environments and feedback signals. The challenge is making sure improvements generalize beyond the particular tasks we train on.

r001.rationale: The response presents post-training as both exposing and developing the base model’s capabilities, and asks how far those capabilities can be pushed—clearly framing it as a way to realize the model’s performance potential.
